entities.name: Alpha Bank
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Alpha Bank, founded 1879 in Kalamata, Greece by Ioannis F. Costopoulos, is one of Greece's four systemic banks — a major lender that survived the Greek financial crisis (2010-2018) through recapitalization, asset sales, and loan restructuring, and is now (with €80 billion in assets) one of the most important financial institutions in southeastern Europe. Alpha Bank's history traces Greek economic development from the 19th-century Kingdom of Greece through the 20th-century industrialization and the 21st-century sovereign debt crisis.

The Costopoulos family maintained bank ownership across generations from 1879 through the 20th century, making Alpha Bank Greece's most important family-controlled bank. Alpha Bank's growth through the 20th century tracked Greece's economic expansion: from a Peloponnesian regional bank to a national lender. The 1993-2000 Balkan expansion — establishing operations in Albania, Bulgaria, Serbia, Romania, and Cyprus — positioned Alpha Bank as a southeastern European financial institution.

The 2010-2018 Greek crisis: Greece's sovereign debt crisis triggered a banking crisis — Greek banks held massive amounts of Greek government bonds that were restructured at 50%+ losses (PSI 2012). Alpha Bank required two recapitalizations (2012 and 2015) from the Hellenic Financial Stability Fund, receiving €4+ billion in state support. The bank's non-performing loan (NPL) ratio reached 50%+ at peak crisis; it declined to 8% by 2023 through securitization programs (Project Galaxy, COSMOS). The 2023 partial privatization saw the Greek state's HFSF stake reduced to below 10%.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Alpha Bank's survival through the Greek financial crisis — the most severe banking stress test experienced by a eurozone member state — demonstrates both the fragility of small-economy banks exposed to sovereign debt and the effectiveness of eurozone bailout mechanisms in preserving systemic financial institutions.
